name: TGF-beta growth factor serums

lead: These serums put growth factors, including TGF-beta, in a skincare product. People apply them to improve firmness, texture and fine lines.
They are often used after microneedling or procedures as part of a rejuvenation routine.

paras: Proponents say TGF-beta signals fibroblasts to produce collagen. Delivery through intact skin is a topic formulators discuss.
They are cosmetics, so claims are not pre-approved [1]. Irritation is possible; patch testing is commonly recommended on labels.

chain: Serum delivers growth factors to the skin surface

angle.text: Users apply these serums daily to improve fine lines, texture and firmness. They are often used after microneedling or in-clinic procedures as part of a skin-rejuvenation routine.

lead: TGF-beta growth factor serums are topical skincare products that contain transforming growth factor beta, often alongside other growth factors, in a cosmetic base. People use them to make skin look firmer and smoother, with the stated aim of encouraging the skin's collagen-producing cells and slowing the sagging and fine lines associated with ageing.

Growth factors are naturally occurring signalling proteins that stimulate cell growth and wound healing; platelets, for instance, release PDGF, IGF-1, EGF and TGF-beta, which attract and activate macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelial cells at a wound.[1] TGF-beta has three main isoforms in mammals and is part of normal tissue repair. Wikipedia's TGF-beta article notes that it contributes to skin ageing by reducing subcutaneous fat, which leads to sagging and wrinkles, and that it stops dermal fibroblasts from becoming fat cells.[2]

Many such serums source growth factors from cultured skin cells or their conditioned medium. They are sold as cosmetics; the term cosmeceutical is used for such products, and Wikipedia notes that US law does not recognise it as a category and that a product with drug properties must be approved as a drug.[3] Published trials on specific serums are limited.

paras: Growth factor serums are used on the face for anti-ageing, texture and post-procedure skin care. TGF-beta is among the factors linked to extracellular matrix and tissue repair in skin biology, which is the basis for its inclusion.[1][2]

Proponents say topical TGF-beta signals fibroblasts to make collagen and other matrix proteins. TGF-beta is secreted in a latent form bound to proteins in the extracellular matrix and is activated by proteases, integrins and other factors, which means its action in tissue is tightly regulated.[2] Whether large protein molecules reach the dermis through intact skin is discussed by formulators, and some products pair serums with microneedling to improve delivery.

Microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy, punctures the skin with fine needles and is used for scarring and acne; Wikipedia notes research is ongoing and that combinations with platelet-rich plasma, which may contain growth factors, remain in question pending studies.[4]

Wikipedia notes that in the US cosmetic products have no legal requirement to prove their claims, and that the term cosmeceutical can lead consumers to assume drug-level testing.[3] TGF-beta also has roles in scarring and fibrosis, and in cancer biology it can promote tumour progression when its control pathways are disrupted;[2] these roles concern signalling inside tissue rather than cosmetic use, and no study located addresses cosmetic serums. Users commonly patch test new serums.

The microneedling article reports serious infection-control concerns when needling and blood-derived treatments are done in non-medical settings, including a 2024 CDC report of three women diagnosed with HIV after vampire facials at one Albuquerque spa.[4]
